Chapter 29

Multiplayer Games

Chapter 29 of Chen & Ankenman's The Mathematics of Poker: why "optimal" stops meaning anything when a third player sits down. A light treatment by design — the chapter's own message is that these games have equilibria but no solutions.

Why three is different

Nash proved every finite game has an equilibrium — a strategy set no one can profit by unilaterally leaving. But in multiplayer games equilibria multiply (chicken has three, with utterly different characters), and nothing stops two players from jointly drifting into an alliance that farms the third. "Hard" collusion breaks the rules; "soft" collusion — implicit, no information shared — is just… poker. The three toy games below (verified in verify.py) each isolate one facet.

1 · The rock & the maniac: a fair game you cannot win

Three players ante $10, one card each; aces and kings win. The player on your left announces: "check always, call only with a winner." The one on your right: "bet $30 always, call always." Both exploitable-looking, both fully disclosed, and the game is symmetric. Your best response (call with everything — folding a loser gives 0, calling nets +$1.87) still loses:

Your cardOpponentsNetProb.EV
winnerboth winners$00.25%0
winnerrock W, maniac L+$201.86%+$0.372
winnerrock L, maniac W+$51.86%+$0.093
winnerboth losers+$5011.41%+$5.707
loserboth losers+$559.93%+$2.996
loserany winner−$4024.69%−$9.875
total−$0.707

The rock and the maniac form an implicit alliance without exchanging a bit of information: the maniac charges you $30 to see a showdown, and the rock only ever puts money in when he has you beat. The book conjectures real three-handed analogues exist — two players whose pre-announced strategies make the third's EV negative.

2 · The dry side pot: bluffing changes meaning

X and Y with chips, Z all-in; pot 9; hands uniform on [0,1]; one half street. A successful "bluff" no longer wins the pot — Z can't fold — so it's really a semi-bluff that evicts X and then must beat Z. The equilibrium (book's own indifference system: y₁ = x/2, w = x/(20−18x), w = √((1+x)² − 40x/9), solved correctly and confirmed by a 2000-point no-deviation check):

value bet [0, .259]
check
bluff .759±.024
check
X calls [0, 0.518]
X folds

Erratum: the book reports x ≈ 0.2848, y₁ ≈ 0.1424, bluff band 0.6424 ± 0.0095 — values that don't satisfy its own three equations (they give w = 0.019 on one side and 0.620 on the other), and against which Y could profitably bluff hand 0.5 for +0.68. The true simultaneous root is x = 0.5178, y₁ = 0.2589, band 0.7589 ± 0.0242. The chapter's qualitative points survive: X calls far less than the 9/10 he would without Z, and the bluff-to-value ratio (0.187) runs above the two-player α = 1/10. And the destabilizing lesson stands: if Y overbluffs, he transfers X's equity to Z — allying with the all-in player — and X's best recourse hands some equity back to Y.

3 · The clairvoyant maniac: announce your sins

Z is clairvoyant into a pot of 9 against X and Y, who hold identical hands and can only check/call. In equilibrium Z bluffs α = 1/10 per value bet and gets called 9/10 of the time in total. Now let Z announce a bluff ratio β and let X and Y respond greedily:

announced bluffs per value bet: β =
X's response
Y's response
Z's EV per value bet
alliance formed

Z's EV per value bet is discontinuous in his announced bluff ratio. Bluff a little too much (β just over 1/10) and X snaps off every bluff: Z bleeds. But bluff three times the equilibrium rate and Y — who could never overcall at equilibrium — finally has odds to overcall behind X: Z collects two bets on every value hand, 17/10 per value bet instead of 9/10. Over-bluffing only works if the victims know about it: the equilibrium is disturbed into an alliance of Z with whichever opponent his β recruits. This is the chapter's closing idea — and why the book refuses to say "optimal" about multiplayer poker at all.
